35. It appears that the Rule was issued by the High Court Division upon the respondents, who are the appellants before us, to show cause as to why sanction given by the respondent No.2, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs Government of Bangladesh, vide Memo No. স্বঃ মঃ (আইন-১)/জক্ষরি-১/০৭(অংশ-৫)/৭১২ dated 16-7-2007 purportedly under Rule 19(ঞ) (2) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, for proceeding with Gulshan Police Station Case No. 34 dated 13-6-2007 filed under sections 385/109 of the Penal Code, 1860, under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, treating the offence alleged to be of public importance, evidenced by the Annexure C to the writ petition, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 39. In the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 319 this Court held: 

 42. Excepting the proceedings in habeas corpus all other types of writ petition are civil proceedings. In the case of Moni Begum vs RAJUK reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154 this Court held that the proceedings in any writ jurisdiction are civil proceedings and, in such view of the matter, the provision of Order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure shall apply in respect of matters not covered by the High Court Division Rules 1960 by virtue of section 117 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Reference may be made of the case of Hussain Baksh vs Settlement Commissioner reported in 21 DLR 456 and therefore we hold that in a writ proceeding like the present one the provision of Order VII, rule 7 ought to have been followed. 

 43. In the case of Hefzur Rahman (Md) vs Shamsun Nahar Begum reported in 51 DLR (AD) 172 the plaintiff neither made out any case in the plaint claiming maintenance till remarriage nor prayed for any relief specifically in that behalf. But the learned Judges of the High Court Division suo malo posed themselves the question, whether the wife could have claimed maintenance beyond the period of iddat and allowed maintenance beyond the period of iddat. 

 59. In the case of Mohammad Alam vs State reported in 19 DLR (SC) 242 Pakistan Supreme Court held as under: 

 61. In the case of Abdul Wadud vs State reported in 48 DLR (AD) 6 it was held that if a statute deals merely with the procedure in an action, and does not affect the rights of the parties, it will be held to apply prima facie, to all actions pending as well as future. But the principle is that procedural laws are always retrospective unless a different intention is manifestly expressed in the statute itself. 

 63. Similar view was taken by this Court in the case of AKM Azizul Islam vs State reported in 49 DLR (AD) 115 and it was held in that case: 

 66. Neither the EP Ordinance nor the EPR has made sections 385/109 an offence. It was an offence since the enactment of Penal Code in 1860 and this offence is not a creation of EPR. What the EPR 14 has done is that it has brought the said offence within the mischief of Rule 14 for the purpose of trial by the Court set up under the EPR. Therefore, it cannot be said that EPR has made it punishable in 2007 but it was not at all offence before 2007 or 2000 or 2001 when the offence was allegedly committed. This was an offence under sections 385/109 and it has only been made triable under the EPR. Therefore, by no stretch of imagination there has been any violation of the Rules against ex post facto law as provided for by Article 35(1) of the Constitution. 

 69. The Emergency Power Ordinance provides for this power of bringing any offence committed before or after Ordinance triable under the Emergency Power Rules. It is true that the Rules 3 to 8 of the Emergency Power Rules created .certain offences and provide for their punishment and mode of trial and therefore, offences so created are prospective and cannot be punished for activities mentioned in the sections if committed prior to 12th of January, 2007. But that does not mean that the offences mentioned in Rules 14 and 15 providing for trial of offences under various laws are prospective, inasmuch as Rules 14 and 15 simply brought those offences within the mischief of Emergency Power Rules only for the purpose of trial but the offences mentioned therein were offences since the promulgation of the respective laws and in the instant case, we have already held, that the offence of section 385 is as old as Penal Code itself which came into being in 1860. 

 71. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel for the respondent, has referred to and the High Court Division relied upon the case of Registrar, University of Dhaka vs Dr Syed Sajjad Hussain reported in 34 DLR (AD) 1 wherein it was held that President's Order No. 67 of 1972 was prospective and further held that the Act had the protection of Article 35 of the Constitution. We have no hesitation in holding that though President's Order No. 67 of 1972 was prospective but it neither required any protection under Article 35 of the Constitution nor it was entitled to get such protection under Article 35 for the simple reason that Article 35 is not applicable in the cases of civil liabilities. 

 96. Bail is therefore a privilege granted by the Court to any accused and not a right. The provision of bail is provided in the Code of Criminal Procedure in sections 496, 497, 498 and 426 thereof and in bailable offences Court will grant bail as a matter of course but in non-bailable offences bail is never a right and it is sometimes granted in appropriate cases as a privilege. Same view was expressed by Thomas M Cooley in his Treatis on the Constitutional Limitations 1868 where he wrote: 

 97. This Court dealt upon the bail matter in the Case of Anti-Corruption Commission vs Barrister Mir Mohammad Helaluddin and Barrister Nazmul Huda reported in 60 DLR (AD) 57 and Criminal Appeal No. 65 of 2007 and no further discussion is called for here. 

 98. Before the High Court Division the very Rule was with regard to the sanction given for trial of the respondent vide Memo No. স্বঃ মঃ (আইন-১)/জক্ষবি-১/০১/(অংশ-৫)/৭১২ dated 16-7-2007 purportedly under Rule-19ঞ(1) and (2) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, for proceeding with Gulshan Police Station Case No. 34 dated 13-6-2007 filed under sections 385/109 of the Penal Code, 1860, under the Emergency Power Rules; 2007, treating the offence alleged to be of public importance, evidenced by the Annexure C to the writ petition. 

 102. We find substance in this submission and we find that there is nothing wrong in giving the sanction in exercise of the power given under Rule 19ঞ of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007. Sometimes the status of the accused is considered in criminal proceedings. In the case of PD Patel vs Emperor reported in 1 ITR (1933) P 363 the status of Patel was considered and only because he was a Barrister his sentence was enhanced and in the case of SA Maquith Chowdhury vs State reported in 11 DLR (SC) 105 the Pakistan Supreme Court did not reduce the sentence only because the accused was an Advocate. 

 1. That the sanction given by the respondent No. 2, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh vide Memo No. স্বঃ মঃ (আইন-১)/জক্ষবি-১/০৭/(অংশ-৫)/৭১২ dated 16-7-2007 purportedly under Rule-19ঞ (2) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, for proceeding with Gulshan Police Station Case No, 34 dated 13-6-2007 filed under sections 385/109 of the Penal Code, 1860, under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, treating the offence to be of public importance, evidenced by the Annexure C to the writ petition, does not suffer from any illegality or infirmity and is a valid sanction in the eye of law. 

 6.The case of Registrar, University of Dhaka vs Dr Syed Sajjad Hussain reported in 34 DLR (AD) 1 was correctly decided but the reference to Article 35 was not correct and was done inadvertently as PO No. 67 of 1972 did not create any offence.
